verdict.headline: Iran makes its Hormuz offer public, and oil, bond yields and rate-hike bets ease before the open
verdict.label: Pre-market: S&P 500 futures +0.31-0.4%, Nasdaq 100 futures +0.61-0.7%; 10Y ~5.17% (-3 bp); 30Y 5.48% Thu close; October hike odds 71% from 77.5%; Brent ~$105 (-1%); gold ~$4,268; BTC ~$85,200; Nikkei 66,364 +1.3%
verdict.rationale_short:
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi made the Hormuz offer public overnight as a seven-day plan to reopen the strait and restart nuclear talks. The seven days start only when Washington accepts Tehran's conditions: at least $12 billion of frozen assets released, a waiver on Iranian oil sanctions and the end of the US naval blockade. On Thursday stocks moved on a Reuters report of the talks while bonds and oil barely reacted. This morning bonds and oil are moving in the same direction as stocks. Brent is about 1% lower, the ten-year is about 3 basis points lower near 5.17%, and CME FedWatch October hike odds fell to 71% from 77.5%. S&P 500 futures are up 0.31-0.4% and Nasdaq 100 futures 0.61-0.7%, with chipmakers and Akamai leading.

The pullback is small next to the move it follows. The ten-year has given back about 3 of the more than 20 basis points it gained over two sessions. Brent has taken back less than a third of Thursday's 3.4% gain. Reuters puts Thursday's thirty-year close at 5.4816%, above the 5.46% carried in last night's report, so the break of the 5.44% 2007 high was wider than first reported. The Nikkei rose 1.3% with Japanese banks up about 4% as yields there eased too, which fits a global inflation premium coming off a little, not a US-specific problem being solved.

What would change the picture: a thirty-year close back under 5.40% would mean the bond market has accepted the equity market's reading of the Iran news. A close at or above 5.48% with Brent lower would mean the long end is being driven by supply and term premium more than by oil. A US acceptance of the plan would start a seven-day clock and could take Brent under $100. Silence past the September 29 end of the reported window would leave this morning's gains resting on an offer, not an agreement.
verdict.lede_short: Iran made its Hormuz offer public as a seven-day plan, but the clock starts only if Washington accepts conditions including $12 billion in frozen assets and an oil-sanctions waiver. Oil fell about 1%, the ten-year about 3 basis points and October hike odds to 71% from 77.5%, while Nasdaq futures rose about 0.6%. Those moves undo only a small part of this week's rise. A thirty-year close back under 5.40% would show the bond market accepting the stock market's view of the Iran news.

supporting_data.label: Iran's foreign minister said Hormuz 'will be open at the end of seven days' if Washington accepts conditions including at least $12 billion of frozen assets, an oil-sanctions waiver and the end of the naval blockade — more than the US has offered in public, so the clock has not started
CME FedWatch puts October hike odds at 71%, down from 77.5% after Williams on Thursday, while Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.61% — the rate path is easing with oil, not with anything a Fed official said

Oil fell Friday on the prospect of a phased US-Iran deal, with Brent about 1% lower after Thursday's 3.4% gain to $106.60 — the market has taken back less than a third of that rise, a more cautious reading than stocks gave the news

The thirty-year Treasury yield rose 7.96 basis points to 5.4816% on Thursday, its highest since 2004 — the level any pullback today is measured against, and further above the 5.44% 2007 high than first reported

Akamai is up about 20% premarket on a seven-year, $11.6 billion Anthropic commitment that includes a warrant for about 5% of the shares at $111.33 — AI-infrastructure spending is being priced higher even with the ten-year above 5%
The Nikkei 225 rose 1.3% to 66,364 for a fifth straight gain, with Japanese banks up about 4% as the global bond selloff eased — the relief is global, the same trade as in Treasuries

watchlist_mentions.note: Up about 2% premarket, extending a week-long run tied to Meta's Muse agent and the case for more CPUs in AI data centers. AMD crossed $1 trillion in market value on Thursday. Its reported price increase takes effect October 1.
Rose about 3% Thursday on Muse adoption. Goldman Sachs estimates 100 million Muse users would need 1.6-1.7 gigawatts of compute, which is the demand case behind this week's CPU-maker rally.
Reports fiscal Q4 on September 30, the same day as August PCE. Akamai's Anthropic-linked capex increase includes memory, and October hike odds eased to 71% this morning.

trade_setups.thesis: The long bond closed Thursday at 5.4816%, above the 5.44% 2007 high, and is lower this morning as oil eases on Iran's public Hormuz offer. The ten-year has given back about 3 of more than 20 basis points gained over two sessions, so the relief is small next to the move.
trade_setups.entry: Thirty-year 5.48% Thursday close against the 5.44% 2007 high and 5.40%; ten-year about 5.17%.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close back under 5.40% would mean bonds have accepted the equity market's reading of the Iran news. A close at or above 5.48% with Brent lower would point to supply and term premium rather than oil.

trade_setups.thesis: Brent is about 1% lower near $105 after Iran published a seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz. The clock starts only on US acceptance of conditions including at least $12 billion of frozen assets and an oil-sanctions waiver, so oil is pricing an offer, not an agreement.
trade_setups.entry: Brent about $105 against Thursday's $106.60 settle and the $100 level.
trade_setups.invalidation: A US acceptance that starts the clock would put $100 in play. No response past the September 29 end of the reported window would leave the premium in place.

trade_setups.thesis: Akamai is up about 20% premarket on a seven-year, $11.6 billion Anthropic commitment that could expand by about $9 billion, with a warrant for about 5% of the stock at $111.33 and a matching capex increase.
trade_setups.entry: The $111.33 warrant strike and the size of the opening gap.
trade_setups.invalidation: A fade of most of the gap within the week would mean the market is weighing the capex and dilution more than the revenue. Holding the gap into Micron's print would mean it is being priced as AI-infrastructure demand.
